/environment/2026/oct/21/energy-secretar.headline: Climate campaigners condemn ‘maddening’ decision to approve Jackdaw gasfield
/environment/2026/oct/21/energy-secretar.excerpt: Climate campaigners and green experts have condemned the government’s decision to allow the drilling of the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. They said approval for the site would jeopardise the UK’s climate targets, fail to reduce the cost of living, and distract from the need to decarbonise the UK’s energy sector. Many drew parallels with the record-breaking heatwave and drought, fuelled by global heating, that the UK experienced this summer. “Is the prime minister living in a parallel universe? One where we haven’t just endured our hottest summer on record, with droughts, wildfires and, in all likelihood, the most heat-related deaths on record?” said Danny Gross, climate campaigner for Friends of the Earth. “And where the UN hasn’t warned that we’re on the brink of breaching the all-important 1.5C warming limit?” As the gas from Jackdaw will be sold on international markets, Gross said it would not bolster the UK’s energy security, but would add to global greenhouse gas emissions. “The disconnect [between the government’s green ambitions and its actions] is maddening,” he said. “This benefits oil giants and their shareholders and doesn’t make life more affordable as Burnham promised,” said Tessa Khan, the executive director of the campaigning organisation Uplift.
/environment/2026/oct/21/energy-secretar.trail: Critics say move will jeopardise climate targets, fail to cut cost of living and distract from need to decarbonise energy

/environment/2026/oct/21/energy-secretar.headline: Tuesday briefing: To drill or not to drill – Burnham’s first big climate test
/environment/2026/oct/21/energy-secretar.excerpt: Good morning. What a difference a new job can make. “To have a shot at staying within 1.5C global warming, we can’t have any new oil or gasfields … It’s irresponsible and shortsighted to be funding new #fossilfuels when we need to be getting to #NetZero.” This was the 2022 message from Miatta Fahnbulleh, now the secretary of state for energy security and net zero. It’s a testament to her remarkable rise that Fahnbulleh wasn’t even an MP when she posted it four years ago. Today, she is in the cabinet, facing (or is the face of, at least) one of the most challenging, and potentially controversial questions looming for the new government: to drill or not to drill, baby? Two sites are the focus of fierce debate. Yesterday, a public consultation on whether to greenlight extraction at one of them – Jackdaw – closed. Next Monday, it’ll be the same for the other, Rosebank. Andy Burnham has been silent about the climate crisis since taking office. As we enter yet another heatwave, what his government does next will be a defining signal of intent on the issue. But what would extraction actually mean, and how many options are open to Fahnbulleh? That’s the subject of today’s First Edition, after a roundup of this morning’s headlines. Five big stories Colombia | More than 100 people have died after a powerful earthquake struck western Colombia, collapsing and severely damaging scores of buildings in major cities including Cali and Pereira.
/environment/2026/oct/21/energy-secretar.trail: In today’s newsletter: As we enter our fifth summer heatwave, Andy Burnham’s government is looking at what the UK should do with its remaining North Sea oil and gas

/environment/2026/oct/21/energy-secretar.headline: Sadiq Khan calls on Andy Burnham to commit to climate action as pressure grows over North Sea oil
/environment/2026/oct/21/energy-secretar.excerpt: Sadiq Khan has called on the government to commit to revamped climate action and to reduce the UK’s reliance on oil and gas, as the UK endures a summer of drought, wildfires and heatwaves. Writing in the Guardian, the mayor of London said that Andy Burnham’s administration must reaffirm its commitment to net zero and make clear it will continue to reduce the UK’s reliance on oil and gas “to get Britain back on track.” There is growing concern among Labour MPs and climate experts that the new prime minister may support renewed drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea; since arriving in No 10, Burnham has remained largely tight-lipped on climate and environmental concerns despite speaking out about them during his time as mayor of Greater Manchester. Last month, Burnham said he would be “pragmatic” about oil and gas and that decisions on new drilling would be made “in due course”. “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is where does it come from,” he said. Khan writes that, faced with the realities of a rapidly worsening climate crisis, which has amplified heatwaves and droughts sweeping across the UK and Europe, governments must redouble their efforts. “National governments across the globe must step up and meet the gravity of this moment with renewed focus, funding, and resolve,” said Khan. A decision on whether to approve more drilling in the North Sea is expected in the coming weeks.
/environment/2026/oct/21/energy-secretar.trail: London mayor points to ‘terrifying scenes’ this summer amid speculation Burnham may back Jackdaw and Rosebank projects

/technology/2026/oct/21/flaw-in-php-comp.headline: What are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?
/technology/2026/oct/21/flaw-in-php-comp.excerpt: Warnings about what artificial intelligence might do in the future – together with alarming reports of what it has gotten up to already – are being issued so quickly that even security experts have difficulty triaging what to worry about. Yet a report this week from Anthropic’s offensive research team grabbed attention by describing a new, practical threat, one devoid of human characteristics or apocalyptic musings. The red team, as such internal testers are called, said it created a malicious AI program that spread autonomously through internet-connected “smart” televisions and could do the same inside other ordinary devices. While machines running AI usually need a fair amount of computing power, the researchers said that their program split parts of itself among 15 televisions and was still able to function by using a bit of power from each. In addition to evoking the horcruxes that kept pieces of Lord Voldemort’s soul alive within objects in the Harry Potter series, the report alarmed some professionals because the generally weak security of smart televisions and many other “internet of things” devices would be very hard to correct, even with a concerted effort. “It’s something to worry about just like every other wave of cyber-attacks. We need to mitigate the possible effects,” said Joshua Saxe, who led development of Meta’s AI security effort.
/technology/2026/oct/21/flaw-in-php-comp.trail: The tech company says successful AI worms need more capability on less powerful devices, but current trends make that feasible by the end of the year

/technology/2026/oct/21/flaw-in-php-comp.headline: Cyber-attack similar to OpenAI Medicare breach seems likely in UK, says minister
/technology/2026/oct/21/flaw-in-php-comp.excerpt: An AI-driven cyber-attack similar to the OpenAI breach of Australia’s healthcare system is likely, “if not inevitable”, in the UK, according to a senior minister. Kanishka Narayan, the UK AI minister, indicated that the British government’s own cyber defences would be bypassed by a technology that has developed highly sophisticated skills in cybersecurity. In a speech Narayan said an incident in June when an OpenAI agent – a computer program acting autonomously – infiltrated Medicare, Australia’s universal healthcare system, could be repeated in the UK. “It concerns me,” he said. “It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached.” Narayan said the agent’s task was “benign” as it searched for information about public spending on medicines, but it nonetheless went after data that it was not authorised to have. “The Australian government has said that no personal medical records are known to have been accessed, and there is no evidence of wider compromise, but the incident should concern us,” he said. Speaking at a science and tech hub at Imperial College London, Narayan said the security minister, Dan Jarvis, would lead a government programme to strengthen against cyber-attacks, including from AI. The government will also consider using the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill as a vehicle for introducing AI safety regulations, including making it mandatory to report AI safety incidents.
/technology/2026/oct/21/flaw-in-php-comp.trail: Kanishka Narayan, concerned by Australian incident, says British cyber defences could be bypassed by artificial intelligence agent

/technology/2026/oct/21/flaw-in-php-comp.headline: Asos warns customer data may be compromised after ‘unauthorised’ app access
/technology/2026/oct/21/flaw-in-php-comp.excerpt: Asos is investigating unauthorised access to its app system after shoppers received a notification claiming hackers had “fully compromised” its data. The online fashion retailer said basic personal information including name and contact details might have been accessed by an unidentified third party but it did not believe payment card records or passwords had been compromised. It said in a statement: “We are investigating unauthorised activity involving third-party platforms that we use to communicate with customers. We took immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms and are working with our internal and external specialist advisers, as well as all relevant authorities. “Our website and app are operating as normal, with no current disruption to any aspects of our operations. Customer trust is incredibly important to us, and if the situation changes an update will be provided as appropriate.” It later apologised directly to customers, saying: “We’re sorry that you may have received an unauthorised push notification from us earlier today. Please disregard the notification and do not click or engage with the external third-party link it contained.” The value of Asos’s shares on the London Stock Exchange dived more than 14% after thousands of customers received a notification titled “Asos hacked” with a link that sent them to the Telegram messaging service.
/technology/2026/oct/21/flaw-in-php-comp.trail: Shares in fashion company fall nearly 10% after its app systems are accessed by ‘unidentified third party’

/technology/2026/oct/21/flaw-in-php-comp.headline: Sensitive UK police data vulnerable to ‘compromise’ by US government and foreign actors
/technology/2026/oct/21/flaw-in-php-comp.excerpt: Vast troves of highly sensitive police data are lying on Microsoft cloud platforms which an oﬃcial UK security assessment deemed to be vulnerable to “compromise” by foreign actors and the US government, a Guardian investigation can reveal. The files include criminal records, victim statements, internal emails and sensitive information held by more than 40 police forces across the UK. Some files exceed “oﬃcial” classification, according to a police document seen by the Guardian, raising the possibility the information could be classed as “secret” or “top secret”. The cloud platform is Microsoft Azure, one of the main commercial offerings of the US tech company. It is used by businesses and governments globally and rests on a web of IT infrastructure – datacentres, networking gear, fibre optic cables – that spans more than 100 countries. In recent years, doubts have surfaced about how cloud platforms store data and whether they are truly secure. British police decided to put some of their most sensitive data on the Microsoft platform in a 2017 meeting, a record of which was examined by the Guardian. In doing so, officers accepted that “US government insiders” would be able to see the data, and that it could be “transmitted worldwide”, with “the extent of this … unknown”. According to five specialists who reviewed the Guardian’s findings, the risks identified in that document persist today.
/technology/2026/oct/21/flaw-in-php-comp.trail: Exclusive: Official UK security assessment found Microsoft cloud platform storing files was at potential risk from hostile hackers

/politics/2026/oct/22/aneurin-bevans-per.headline: The power of AI is worrying senior Labour figures – as is the fear of ‘falling behind the public’
/politics/2026/oct/22/aneurin-bevans-per.excerpt: “I have this sense that, within a few months, AI is going to be all anyone is talking about,” said one cabinet minister, with an ominous stare. It was Labour conference, with everyone from ministers to activists jubilant at Andy Burnham’s takeover and a bounce in the polls after the change of leader. But a number of senior Labour figures were privately starting to name the power of AI as the thing worrying them most, alongside the immediate pressures on the cost of living and fragile economy. One cabinet minister – with a brief unrelated to technology – told the Guardian that dangerous, out-of-control AI was the issue keeping them up at night, fretting about the threat to humanity. It was “not killer robots” causing the worry, they explained, but the idea of a huge amount of concentrated, super-intelligent power potentially ending up in the hands of bad actors. Another expressed concern that the government was “falling behind the public” in terms of dealing with worries about AI safety – and that it needed to catch up fast. In his conference speech, Ed Miliband was the most strident about the “daunting” dangers of AI, making the case that politicians could not and would not allow the profits of tech companies “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”. And it has not taken long for these alarm bells to ring even louder, with the last seven days looking like the week Westminster fully woke up to the warnings.
/politics/2026/oct/22/aneurin-bevans-per.trail: Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actors

/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.headline: Former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson sentenced to 15 years for child sexual offences
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.excerpt: Jeffrey Donaldson has been sentenced to 15 years for sexual offences against two women who were children when he abused them, completing what was described as a “catastrophic descent into disgrace”. The sentence at Newry crown court on Thursday sealed the downfall of a former Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader who once dominated unionism in Northern Ireland. Donaldson, 63, was sentenced to 11 years for rape against complainant B and four years for offences against complainant A, to be served consecutively. He is to remain on the sex offender register indefinitely. He had reached the “very height of public office” before a “catastrophic descent into disgrace”, the judge, Paul Ramsey, said. The former Lagan Valley MP had shown no remorse or empathy, said the judge. “There has not been, and doubtless will not be, one word of regret, apology or shame from this man to at least provide his victims with some crumb of comfort.” Ramsey paid tribute to the victims, who were in court. “It is only through the courage, resourcefulness and determination of two young women that you’ve been brought to justice in respect of the crimes you committed against them when they were children,” he said. The head of the Public Prosecution Service’s serious crime unit, Catherine Kierans, lauded the victims’ courage in coming forward to seek justice. “Jeffrey Donaldson held a prominent public position,” she said.
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.trail: Donaldson was found guilty in June of 18 counts of sexual abuse including one rape between 1985 and 2008

/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.headline: Drumcree march standoff: protesters and Orange Order both vow to stay ‘as long as it takes’
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.excerpt: Half a mile of countryside separates Drumcree parish church and Garvaghy Road. You can walk it in 15 minutes, listening to birdsong. The protesters gathered at each end, however, speak of grievances that go back decades and centuries to explain why a dispute once thought settled has returned to torment Northern Ireland. Up on the hill at Drumcree this week, Paul, a 64-year-old Orangeman who declined to give his surname, said for too long he and his brethren had been denied the right to parade along a traditional route that would honour Protestant forefathers who fell at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690 and the Somme in 1916. “The people of Garvaghy have nothing to fear from 35 mostly elderly gentlemen. We’re not out to cause fear or offence to anybody. We just want the rule of law to be applied.” It was a shame, he said, that Garvaghy’s Catholic residents were beholden to “militant voices”. Fellow members of Portadown district Orange Lodge No 1 – once labelled the “Vatican of Orangeism” – take turns staffing a tent filled with supplies. Some wear union jack stickers. How long will they stay? “As long as it takes,” said Paul. The mood at Garvaghy Road, also bedecked with tents, was equally determined. “It’s not about 35 men walking down this road, it’s about what they represent – sectarian domination and triumphalism,” said Tomás Óg McKinney, 57. “How long will we stay? As long as it takes.
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.trail: As members of Orange Lodge No 1 gather and residents occupy Garvaghy Road, each side speaks of grievances that go back decades and centuries

/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.headline: Absence of violence in Drumcree does not make standoff any less significant
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.excerpt: Three decades ago, it took the deaths of three children from a Roman Catholic family – the Quinn brothers, Jason, nine, Mark, 10, and 11-year-old Richard – in a petrol bomb attack to bring an end to the Drumcree dispute. “No road is worth a life, let alone the lives of three little boys,” the Orange Order’s County Armagh chaplain said at the time. It is perhaps extraordinary to think that this could ever have needed saying – but that was then. Northern Ireland is very different place today. Passions are running high, but the attempt by 35 members of the Protestant Orange Order to walk down Garvaghy Road, a main thoroughfare in a predominantly nationalist part of Drumcree in Portadown, County Armagh, did not lead to violence on Sunday or Monday. Faced with thousands of members of the nationalist community standing in their way and a police line ordering them back, Orange Order district master Nigel Dawson concluded: “There’s no point getting wet unnecessarily,” as he instructed members of the order back inside the church hall to shelter from the rain. Every half-hour on Monday, the Orange Order members walked up to police lines only to be turned back by Supt Brendan Green, but the process was peaceful and respectful. The blessed absence of the old ways does not make what is happening at Drumcree any less significant, however. History doesn’t repeat itself, and although hope and history sometimes rhyme, more often we hear echoes of history returning to us.
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.trail: Row comes amid rising division and a tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland

/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.headline: Tensions rise as Orange Order members vow to continue with march blocked by police
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.excerpt: Tensions between unionist and nationalist leaders in Northern Ireland have escalated as a number of Orange Order members remain at Drumcree church, vowing not to leave until they can proceed with their march down a nationalist road in Portadown. Members of the loyalist Orange Lodge made a third attempt to proceed down Garvaghy Road at 4am on Monday morning, but a line of police Land Rovers blocked their path. While protesters at the head of Garvaghy Road were dispersed late last night, there are fears that the tensions between Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) have reached a level that could lead to the collapse of power sharing at Stormont. Speaking to the Irish broadcaster RTÉ on Monday morning, Claire Hanna, the leader of the Social Democratic and Labour party, said collapsing Stormont “solves nothing” as it would halt critical decision-making. “Too often, we have reached for these collapse mechanisms only to have to come back six months later,” she said. The leader of the Ulster Unionist party, Jon Burrows, also said he did not “want to see the executive fall”. He told the BBC: “There are people waiting for health appointments, there are people that wait too long in A&E, people that wait too long for an ambulance, there are lots of initiatives that [health] minister [Robbie] Butler and his predecessors need delivered.
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.trail: Talks expected on Monday after Sinn Féin leaders join those on streets opposing decision to allow unionist parade for first time since 1998

/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.headline: Jeffrey Donaldson could face more than 10 years in jail for child sexual abuse, court told
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.excerpt: Jeffrey Donaldson, the former leader of the Democratic Unionist party in Northern Ireland, could be sent to prison for more than 10 years over the sexual assault of two women when they were children, a court heard on Friday. The disgraced politician, who headed the DUP between 2021 and 2024, was found guilty of 18 counts of sexual abuse including one count of rape against the women in June. Recounting the case, Rosemary Walsh KC reminded Judge Ramsey how the distress felt by Complainant B while giving evidence was “palpable” in the court room. Referring to a victim statement already with the judge, she told how Complainant B had described the trial as “a terrible experience” and how the abuse she suffered as a child “affected her every day” of her life. Sometimes she struggled so much she “wishes she could die”, Walsh said, adding that as a result of the abuse she “does not know what love and trust really is”. The other victim, Complainant A, wrote in her victim impact statement that she felt her childhood had been “stolen from her” and this had led to feelings of shame and anger. Her sleep and sense of wellbeing were affected to this day and sometimes she felt burnt out from the emotional stress. Walsh spoke of various tariffs for the offences, several of which carried a maximum sentence of two years, but others which carried a maximum sentence of between 10 and 14 years under historical tariffs for crimes, she told the court.
/uk-news/2026/oct/21/jeffrey-donaldson-i.trail: Age difference between former Democratic Unionist party leader and his victims an aggravating factor, say prosecutors

/business/2026/oct/22/waitrose-new-super.headline: Nitrite-free bacon sales boom in UK amid fears over curing chemicals
/business/2026/oct/22/waitrose-new-super.excerpt: Bacon has long been a favourite of carnivores, but there is growing consumer concern about the health risks posed by nitrites, chemicals used to cure meats. While many experts argue there is no evidence processed meat made without nitrites is safer, retailers have responded to consumer concerns by offering “nitrite-free” products to meet demand. Denhay, the Devon hand- dry-cured bacon specialist, has launched two new back bacon lines in 570 Tesco stores from 21 September – Made Without Nitrites Smoked Back Bacon and Made Without Nitrites Unsmoked Back Bacon (both 200g), both priced at £4. Waitrose has doubled its Made Without Nitrites range in the past year, with sales up more than 34%. Sales of its British roast and honey roast hams have risen more than 70% since launching in May, and its unsmoked back bacon is up 22%. Data from Worldpanel by Numerator shows nitrite-free bacon growing steadily while conventional bacon declines, and its share of the fresh bacon category has risen steadily from a small base. In the 52 weeks to 6 September 2026, nitrite-free spend reached £34.8m (up 11.4% year on year) and volumes were up to 2.2m kg (up 8.0%), while spend and volume for conventional bacon was 9.2% and 4.9%, respectively.
/business/2026/oct/22/waitrose-new-super.trail: Shoppers are switching from traditional product despite little evidence alternative is safer

/business/2026/oct/22/waitrose-new-super.headline: Cottage pie and glass of red, anyone? Britons shun salad despite heat in ‘reverse comfort eating’
/business/2026/oct/22/waitrose-new-super.excerpt: Forget a crisp salad and glass of chilled rosé. Enervated Britons are seemingly more likely to crave a rich cottage pie and a robust red in heatwaves. In a trend termed “reverse comfort eating”, Waitrose’s cottage pie sales have soared 110% in the last month and South African red wine is up 68% compared with the same period last year. The surprise spike in demand for winter comfort foods also includes retro chicken, bacon and leek pie (up 41%), chicken korma (up 67%) and chicken and ham gratin (68%). Meanwhile, home cooks are happy standing over the stove despite the sweltering heat, with searches for traditional food classics on the supermarket chain’s recipe site up 67% for toad-in-the-hole, 91% for spaghetti bolognese and 57% for rarebit mac and cheese. Another 1950s staple, along with cottage pie and toad-in-the-hole, trifle is also high on shopping lists, with the supermarket seeing a 100% year-on-year increase in sales of its strawberry version. The food historian and author Seren Charrington-Hollis recently catered for a VIP event at the Llangollen Eisteddfod, where her cottage pies and lamb hotpots were in huge demand – to her surprise, “as it was unbearably hot”, she said. “But they all wanted these home-cooked meals,” she said, adding that the guests were fed up of salads.
/business/2026/oct/22/waitrose-new-super.trail: Nostalgic foods like toad-in-the-hole also in demand at Waitrose as people pivot towards familiarity amid climatic and political upheaval

/world/2026/oct/21/heidi-levine-palestin.headline: Israeli military detain US and UK volunteers in West Bank including Democratic NY politician Brad Lander
/world/2026/oct/21/heidi-levine-palestin.excerpt: The Israeli military has detained about 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including the New York Democratic congressional nominee Brad Lander, several rabbis and Israel’s former deputy attorney general. “I’ve been detained by the IDF, along with a group of rabbis and volunteers,” Lander posted from a bus taking him to a police station. “We were simply harvesting olives in a grove near Nahalin in the West Bank. The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know.” Lander, who is Jewish and an outspoken critic of the Israeli government, describes himself as a liberal Zionist. He believes in the vision of Israel as a safe, Jewish home, but argues that it cannot be a true democracy while it denies Palestinians their human rights and freedom. An ally of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, Lander’s critical approach to Israel was a key factor in his resounding primary victory against Dan Goldman, a prominent supporter of Israel. He condemns Israel’s continued occupation of the West Bank and Gaza, supported the restriction of US military aid to Israel and believes that Israel’s military campaign in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks amounts to genocide. Settler militants have unleashed extreme violence on Palestinians attempting to harvest olives from their trees across the occupied West Bank, and anyone accompanying them.
/world/2026/oct/21/heidi-levine-palestin.trail: About 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers held near Nahalin in West Bank and taken to police station

/world/2026/oct/21/heidi-levine-palestin.headline: Fifth foreign firm pulls out of controversial Israeli cable car project to East Jerusalem
/world/2026/oct/21/heidi-levine-palestin.excerpt: A fifth foreign company has pulled out of a plan to build a cable car from West to East Jerusalem that threatens to involve the seizure of land and property rights from dozens of Palestinian families along its route, but local authorities insist the scheme is proceeding as planned. The project appeared to have stalled for four years until late September, just weeks before Israel’s 27 October elections, when the Jerusalem Development Authority (JDA) issued a notice of intent to award a contract without a public tender to ROPES, a cable car engineering consultancy based in South Tyrol, Italy. However, Stephan Obexer, chief executive of ROPES told the Guardian his company had declined the consultancy work because of another commitment in India. The 1.4km cable car route, approved by the Israeli government in 2019 and upheld by the high court in 2022, would connect West Jerusalem to a planned 16,000 sq metres tourist complex promoted by Elad, a settler organisation seeking to consolidate Israeli control over Palestinian areas of occupied East Jerusalem. The Israeli occupation of the Palestinian territories began in 1967 and the Old City and the rest of the eastern half of Jerusalem were fully annexed in 1980, although they are still considered occupied under international law.
/world/2026/oct/21/heidi-levine-palestin.trail: Rights groups say the planned 1.4km route, which ends at compound run by far-right settler group Elad, will displace Palestinians and reshape the cultural landscape

/world/2026/oct/21/heidi-levine-palestin.headline: Israeli police detain 10 people in rare raid against West Bank settlers
/world/2026/oct/21/heidi-levine-palestin.excerpt: Israeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against settlers, after a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied West Bank including an attack on US photojournalist Heidi Levine, which she described as an “attempted lynching”. She was knocked down, kicked and beaten by a group of masked Israeli men as she covered the olive harvest in a Palestinian village on Friday. The militants broke four vertebrae and a rib, ripped open her finger so it required surgery and left her with lacerations across her body. “I was practically, basically lynched by a gang of Jewish settlers in the area of Ramallah,” Levine said, in an interview with the BBC from her hospital bed on Monday. The day after that assault, Israeli militants armed with sticks and iron bars attacked a group of European diplomats and Palestinians harvesting olives outside the town of Taybeh, assaulting a visiting French mayor, smashing the window of an official car, and causing severe injuries to a young Palestinian man. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, questioned the accounts of Israeli militant violence, ignoring extensive video and witness evidence. He referenced an “alleged attack” on Levine, whose severe injuries were visible in interviews from her hospital bed, and “unproven allegations” the diplomats had been targeted by militants.
/world/2026/oct/21/heidi-levine-palestin.trail: Move comes after US photojournalist and group of European diplomats and Palestinians were assaulted in separate attacks

/world/2026/oct/21/heidi-levine-palestin.headline: Guardian reporter filmed masked militants seconds before West Bank attack on French mayor
/world/2026/oct/21/heidi-levine-palestin.excerpt: Hours after Israeli militants attacked a delegation of European diplomats, French clerics and a visiting mayor in the occupied West Bank, Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, responded by questioning the delegation’s account of the assault. “Serious accusations require serious evidence” was the all-caps headline of a social media post from the office of the prime minister. As news of the attack spread globally there was no pledge to find those accountable and bring them to justice. Instead Netanyahu’s team dismissed video of Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, on the ground grimacing in pain and shock, photos of the smashed window of a diplomatic car, and footage of masked men threatening diplomats and activists with sticks. “These images alone do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility,” the statement said, warning of “concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel”. The prime minister’s office went on to cast doubt on the integrity of senior French, Belgian and Polish diplomats in Jerusalem and clergy from the Catholic church who witnessed and reported the attack. “We call on the public and responsible journalists to demand verifiable evidence, reject hearsay and refuse to turn unproven allegations into a collective indictment of the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria [the occupied West Bank],” it said.
/world/2026/oct/21/heidi-levine-palestin.trail: New video footage of Israeli settler assault on European delegation as Netanyahu attempts to raise doubt

/world/2026/oct/21/heidi-levine-palestin.headline: Israeli settlers attack European diplomats in West Bank
/world/2026/oct/21/heidi-levine-palestin.excerpt: Israeli settler militants have attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of Cambrai in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank, injuring three people and damaging a car, in the latest violent attempt to prevent Palestinians from harvesting olives on their own land. Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground on Saturday. The masked militant shouted “Vive la France” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife, and Vincent Dollmann, archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs. The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls. Settlers first attacked a group working on the lower slopes of hills near Taybeh. As well as stealing olives, they kicked, abused and assaulted a Palestinian woman in her 70s and beat a man so badly he needed six stitches for a head injury. Then they approached the diplomats and Badoux, who was in Taybeh for the launch of a twinning agreement with his town in northern France. During the attack, the militants smashed the window of an armoured car belonging to the Belgian mission.
